# Where AI actually helps (and where it can't) {#sec-appendix-ai-assisted-modeling}













You've probably done this already, or watched a labmate do it: paste a spreadsheet of fluorescence intensities into a chat window and ask "what statistical test should I run?" Back comes a confident answer, a t-test, maybe an ANOVA if there are more than two groups, often with a line like "a p-value below 0.05 would indicate a significant difference." It reads like expertise. It even runs without errors. And it quietly hands you back exactly the ritual this whole book has been trying to talk you out of: a single threshold standing in for a scientific judgment nobody actually made.

That's not a reason to avoid these tools. It's a reason to be precise about what they're actually good at, because "precise" is not the same as "cautious to the point of uselessness." I use an AI assistant most days I write R code, and this book itself was partly built with one, in a very specific and disciplined way I'll describe near the end of this appendix. The goal here isn't to warn you off the tool. It's to draw the line in the right place, so you keep the part that genuinely saves you time and lose the part that quietly does your thinking for you.

## The loop again: where delegation is safe and where it isn't

@sec-bayesian-core-workflow gave you a four-step loop for doing this work honestly: model, infer, check, improve. It turns out to be exactly the right lens for this question too, because each step asks for a different kind of work, and AI is good at some of those kinds and bad at others in a way that doesn't change much from one chatbot generation to the next.






::: {#tbl-ai-loop .cell tbl-cap='The model-infer-check-improve loop, and where an AI assistant can actually carry weight'}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(gt)

gt(data.frame(
  Step = c("Model", "Infer", "Check", "Improve"),
  `What it requires` = c(
    "Proposing a theoretically motivated candidate for the process that generated your data",
    "Translating an already-decided model into working code",
    "Judging whether a fitted model's predictions are good enough for the question you're asking",
    "Deciding what to change, and why, when a check comes back unhappy"
  ),
  `Can an AI assistant do this for you?` = c(
    "No. This is domain knowledge about your biology, not a pattern in code.",
    "Mostly yes. This is the part that's genuinely mechanical.",
    "No, though it can explain what a diagnostic means once you show it the output.",
    "No. This is the same domain judgment as Model, applied to a new problem."
  )
))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

\toprule
Step & What.it.requires & Can.an.AI.assistant.do.this.for.you. \\ 
\midrule\addlinespace[2.5pt]
Model & Proposing a theoretically motivated candidate for the process that generated your data & No. This is domain knowledge about your biology, not a pattern in code. \\ 
Infer & Translating an already-decided model into working code & Mostly yes. This is the part that's genuinely mechanical. \\ 
Check & Judging whether a fitted model's predictions are good enough for the question you're asking & No, though it can explain what a diagnostic means once you show it the output. \\

\end{tabular*}
\end{table}

:::






Two of those four rows are not negotiable, and they're not negotiable for the same reason: nothing about a transformer model trained on text gives it access to what cerebral ischemia does to astrocytes, or to whether a 6.5% tail of implausible posterior predictions matters for the question you're actually asking (the exact judgment call @sec-mcmc-model-checking walked through at length). An assistant can describe the general shape of that reasoning back to you, convincingly, because it has read a great many papers that contain that kind of reasoning. It cannot tell you whether it's true of *your* data, because it has never seen your animals, your protocol, or your field's accumulated, half-written-down sense of what a plausible effect size looks like.

## Where it actually helps

The "infer" row is the real win, and it's worth being specific about what that covers, because "it writes code" undersells it:

-   **Boilerplate and syntax, once you've already decided the model.** You know you want a varying-intercepts model with cells nested in sections nested in animals; getting the `brms` formula syntax exactly right (`(1 | animal/section)` versus `(1 | animal) + (1 | section)`, say) is a place a fast assistant genuinely saves you a trip to the documentation. The decision was yours. The notation was tedious.
-   **Debugging.** Pasting a cryptic Stan warning or an R error message into an assistant and getting a plain-language explanation of what it means is a legitimate, low-risk use. You're not asking it to decide anything; you're asking it to translate.
-   **Explaining unfamiliar output.** "What does Rhat mean" or "why would adapt_delta fix this" are exactly the kind of question @sec-mcmc-model-checking spent a whole chapter answering properly. An assistant can give you a reasonable first-pass explanation of a diagnostic faster than searching through documentation, as long as you then hold that explanation to the same standard as anything else you read: does it match what the textbooks actually say.
-   **Literature retrieval, done the right way.** More on this in a moment, because it's different enough from the other items on this list to deserve its own section.
-   **Catching the exact bug this project has made before.** A chunk copied from one chapter into another without updating the variable names is a real, documented failure mode of writing a book like this one across many forked sessions. Asking an assistant to check whether a chunk actually executes against the variables defined earlier in the same file is a genuinely useful, low-stakes review step, not a judgment call at all.

## Where it quietly fails: a worked example

Here's what a typical AI response to "what model should I fit to compare GFAP intensity between sham and ischemic animals" tends to look like, paraphrased from the kind of answer these tools commonly produce:

> "You can compare the two groups with an independent-samples t-test in R: `t.test(Gfap_Intensity ~ Condition, data = cell_data)`. If p < 0.05, you can conclude there's a significant difference between groups. For a Bayesian approach, you could also fit `brm(Gfap_Intensity ~ Condition, data = cell_data)` using default priors."

Read that against four chapters of this book and count what's missing. There's no frequentist-equivalent note explaining what a confidence interval does and doesn't claim (@sec-intro-applied-modeling). There's a p-value doing exactly the lexicographic gating this book has argued against from its opening pages (@sec-appendix-p-values). The `brm()` call defaults to a flat prior with no acknowledgment that this is itself a choice requiring justification, not a neutral starting point (@sec-priors-regularization). And nowhere does it ask whether the fitted model's predictions actually look like the data you collected (@sec-mcmc-model-checking). None of this is a defect you'd expect a patch or a better prompt to fix. It's the direct consequence of a model trained to produce the most statistically *common* answer, and the most common answer in its training data is the ritualistic one, because that's what decades of papers and textbooks mostly did. The tool isn't being careless. It's being representative of a literature this book is explicitly trying to move you past.

::: callout-important
### The one failure mode that should worry you most in a book with a bibliography

Ask an assistant for a citation supporting some claim, and it will frequently give you one that sounds exactly right: a plausible author, a plausible year, a plausible journal, sometimes a paper that doesn't exist at all. This isn't a rare glitch; it's a structural consequence of how these models generate text; a fabricated citation is built from the same statistical process as a real one, and nothing in the model distinguishes them internally. A fabricated reference in a book that teaches rigor would be its own small scandal. Never add a citation to `references.bib` that you haven't actually located and read.
:::

::: callout-tip
### How this book uses AI, and why that's the model to copy

This book was partly written with AI assistance, under a specific rule laid out in its own project instructions: when a claim needs the authority of an actual textbook, the assistant is told exactly what to ask a source library of Daniel's reference books (through a retrieval tool, NotebookLM), the excerpt comes back as a direct quote, and only then does it get integrated and cited. The assistant never invents the citation from memory. It retrieves a passage from a known, checkable source and waits to be handed the real text. That's the general shape worth copying into your own work: use the tool to *find and retrieve*, not to *recall and assert*. The difference sounds small. It's the entire difference between a citation you can defend and one you can't.
:::

## A short checklist for your own analysis

-   Treat any AI-generated code the way @sec-bayesian-core-workflow asked you to treat your own pipeline before trusting it on real data: test it against a case where you already know the right answer, the same positive-control logic as the simulation-based calibration exercise in that chapter, before you trust it on your real animals.
-   Never let it choose your model family, your prior, or your interpretation of a result. Those are exactly the "Model" and "Check" rows in the table above, and they're yours alone.
-   Read every line of generated code before you run it. Not skim. Read.
-   Verify every citation it gives you against the actual source, every time, with no exceptions for ones that sound obviously right.

## Tools worth knowing about

Specific products change too fast for a printed book to chase, so I'll stay at the level of category rather than brand, with one honest caveat: by the time you read this, some of these names may have been replaced by newer ones doing the same job.

- **General-purpose chat assistants** (the category ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini belong to) are useful for the debugging and explaining items above, used in a single back-and-forth rather than trusted as a standing authority.
- **Coding assistants integrated into your editor** (the category GitHub Copilot and Claude Code belong to) are useful specifically because they see your actual project, your actual data column names, your actual previous chunks, which cuts down on the kind of generic, context-free answer the worked example above illustrated.
- **Retrieval-grounded tools**, like the NotebookLM workflow this book itself uses, are the right category for literature claims specifically, because the answer is anchored to a document you chose rather than generated from the model's general training.
- **R-native packages that bring an assistant into your actual console** (`gander`, `chattr`, and `ellmer` are three worth knowing the names of as of this writing) keep the whole interaction inside your R session instead of a separate browser tab, which matters less for judgment and more for simply not breaking your flow. Check their current state on CRAN before relying on them in your own workflow; packages in this space move quickly.

## The part that doesn't change

Strip away the specific tool names and one thing holds regardless of how good these assistants get: a model is a claim about what process generated your data, and only you can be held responsible for whether that claim is true. AI changes who types the `brm()` call. It doesn't change who has to stand behind what it claims.
